venues.place: A high-street opticians on a school-holiday Wednesday: a frame-display wall and a dispensing bench down one side, two test rooms with their doors hooked open, the lit letter chart at the far end of the test lane, and a low toy table beside the waiting chairs.
venues.activity: Everyone is working through a sight test — reading a line off the chart with one eye covered under a paddle, following the pen-torch with their eyes, sitting up to the phoropter, trying a frame at the mirror while a parent answers the questions across the desk.
venues.anchor_structure: The full-length test lane — the studded carpet strip with the back-lit letter chart standing at its far end and the facing mirror above it — running from the lower-left corner of the frame to the upper right, dividing the shop into waiting chairs, dispensing bench, test lane and the glazing workshop behind.
venues.pun_explanation: M-S-E stands as an ordered subsequence of word-initials inside an utterly ordinary optician's fascia — the expreSS tRIps device — and it is planted in the one high-street trade whose examinees are children of every age with a parent sitting beside them, which is what the vehicle-test version could not supply. The trade then pays out on all five aspects with no invention: a sight test is run in a fixed non-negotiable order, history then acuity then cover test then refraction then the light, so examination structure is the venue's own procedure; the record card carries the child's whole history back to the first visit and the parent supplies it across the desk, so developmental history and parent interview are one piece of counter business; the method changes with age — pictures for the pre-schooler, letters for the schoolchild, a moving toy for the infant who cannot answer — which is the chapter's central teaching point rendered as ordinary shop routine; the optometrist down on the floor rolling a toy for a two-year-old to fix and follow is play observation as a real clinical technique rather than a metaphor; and because every examinee in the frame is an actual child, appearance, speech, mood and behaviour are all literal depiction. The chart's shrinking graded rows are a native developmental ladder and the red recall tabs standing proud of the record drawer are the red flags.

venues.place: A village shop row on delivery morning: one unbroken terrace of small businesses down the near side of the street, the colliery gates and winding gear closing the top of the road, delivery lorries nosed into the kerb with their tailgates down, crates stacked out on the flags outside every doorway.
venues.activity: Everyone is taking in the morning delivery — lifting crates down off the lorries at the kerb, wheeling sack-trucks in through the doorways, signing the docket on the driver's board, and carrying the empties back out to be loaded up again.
venues.anchor_structure: The unbroken run of shopfront fascias with the kerb and gutter line beneath them, running from the lower left of the frame up to the colliery gates at the top right, splitting the picture into pavement, roadway, shopfronts and the upper windows above them.
venues.pun_explanation: A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger, and Messenger Row is an ordinary street nameplate that carries one morpheme of the everyday referent without printing the medical word — the same device the accepted transmitter reading used, and within the Lithium Lift precedent. This is the one chapter the spec says must not invent a venue: the seven course-wide premises are the content, so the plate is the street they stand on. A shop row is the only mundane container that holds a colliery, a hotel, a dairy, a club door, a weaving workshop, a seed merchant and a police box in one coherent frame at one light source. The delivery round then supplies the whole mechanism free: release is a crate carried in off the lorry, and reuptake is the same hand carrying the empties back out to be loaded again, which is a native action in the trade rather than a metaphor. Each premises signs for its own crate, so every messenger stays addressable at its own doorway instead of becoming one of seven nameplated boxes in a line-up.

venues.place: A covered market hall in mid-morning trade: an iron-and-glass roof over one long central aisle, lock-up stalls down both sides with their shutters up, scales and price cards on every counter, produce boxes stacked in the gangway and a wash-down channel running along the floor.
venues.activity: Everyone is doing the market shop — working down the aisle with a basket, asking across the counter, being handed a wrapped parcel, paying, and moving on to the next stall.

venues.pun_explanation: 5-H-T stands as an ordered subsequence of word-initials inside an entirely ordinary market name and street address — the expreSS tRIps device, and a numeral at the front of a market name is native signage rather than an intrusion. The hall was chosen because serotonin's whole story is one narrow midline workshop that ships everywhere, and a market's central aisle is literally its seam: the weaving stall stands on it and its goods go out to every other counter in the building. The receptor family then costs nothing, because each one is an ordinary trade already found in a market hall — a curtained fortune-teller's booth in the corner, the pie stall kitchen behind it, the wash-down channels of the fish end, the second-hand book stall, and the all-night kiosk in the corner arch. The postal collection at the delivery bay gives reuptake a native worker instead of a symbol.

venues.place: A canal lock on a working navigation, mid-morning: the stone chamber with its gates shut at the tail, balance beams swung out over the towpath, a queue of narrowboats waiting down on the low pound below with their propellers half out of the water, and the lock cottage with its porch bench and gauging tape at the top of the steps.
venues.activity: Everyone is working a boat through the lock: winding a paddle up one notch at a time on a windlass, leaning a balance beam round to swing a gate, holding a centre line while the chamber fills, watching the water climb the painted gauge board, and stepping off to set the next one.
venues.anchor_structure: The lock chamber wall itself — the long coursed stone face with its painted gauge board, ladder rungs, green water line and spalled mortar — running from the bottom-left of the frame to the top right, dividing the scene into the starved low pound with its waiting boats, the towpath and beams, the chamber, and the full pound above.
venues.pun_explanation: A lock exists to raise something starved of water back up to level, and the one absolute rule of working one is that you let the water in slowly, a notch at a time — draw all the paddles at once and the chamber boils in, the boat is thrown against the cill and holed. That is refeeding syndrome, drawn as the trade's own cardinal safety rule rather than as a metaphor, and it is the single hardest fact in the chapter to place anywhere else. The sign is the second half of the pun: on a canal a pound is the level stretch of water between two locks, and a pound short of water is the everyday phrase for a level that has run too low to float anything — while in trade a short pound is a pound that weighs less than a pound. One three-word place name that a canal would genuinely carry therefore says low weight twice, in two registers, and never says the diagnosis. The rest of the syllabus falls out of the stock: the subtypes are two boats, one that takes nothing on at all and one that fills its tank and then runs the bilge pump straight back over the side; the gauge board and the boat-gauging tape are the assessment instruments and also the disturbed reading of a hull that plainly fits and is recorded as too wide; bradycardia is the paddle wound at half speed, hypothermia the cold green water, the low electrolytes three low marks on the same board, and osteopenia the crumbling mortar of the chamber wall, which is the only structural thing in the frame and is losing it. Family-based treatment is the strongest image the venue supplies: a family works one boat through with the parents on the paddle gear controlling the rate of filling and the adolescent aboard, which is exactly the transfer of control FBT prescribes. Mortality is carried by the lifebelt, the rescue pole and the plate on the wall, and by the fact that this is the only venue in the batch where the ordinary hazard is drowning.

venues.place: A small municipal observatory in a town park on a public open night: the dome with its slit rolled back over the lawn, a row of borrowed telescopes set out on the grass, the warm room with its log desk and clock board, and the park gate standing open onto the road.
venues.activity: Everyone is observing: bending to an eyepiece and winding the focus, swinging a finder onto a target, holding a red torch over a chart, writing a line into the log book, and cranking the dome round a few degrees to keep up.
venues.anchor_structure: The long white refractor tube on its cast-iron equatorial mount — pier, counterweight, tube and dew shield — running from the lower-left of the frame up and out through the open dome slit at the top right, splitting the scene into the dome floor, the warm room, the observing lawn and the park gate.
venues.pun_explanation: Phase is the same word in both trades: an observatory's whole business is phase, and a delayed phase is the chapter. The name is therefore an exact homonym planted in a place name a real observatory would carry, and it prints no clinical word at all. The choice earns its keep because the venue owns, as ordinary equipment, the two objects that make the adolescent shift explicable rather than merely stated. First, two clocks hang on the same warm-room wall reading different times — sidereal and civil — because the sky keeps a period that is not twenty-four hours; that is the internal clock against the school clock, and the discrepancy is an instrument reading, not a mood. Second, the moonrise table pinned beside them lists a rise time roughly fifty minutes later on every successive line, so the picture contains a printed, native, undeniable object whose whole content is a clock that runs later every day. Nothing else in the course supplies that. Sleep architecture by age is literal depiction inside one shared activity: the smallest visitors swing their scopes all over the sky and never settle, which is REM-heavy infant sleep; the school-age children are the ones standing guard over the hour-long exposure that must not be jogged, which is slow-wave; the adults get short broken looks between clouds. Required hours by age become the booking board of session lengths, a properly numbered carrier. The venue is also open at night in a town, which is the only reason the fixed 24-hour store can stand across the road without contrivance — and the sixth-formers drifting out of the gate towards it while everyone else is packing up is the phase delay and its consequence in one movement.

venues.place: A small candle works with its dipping room open to the street on a seaside town's back parade, late afternoon: a row of heated wax vats down the middle, frames of wicks hanging over them from the overhead rail, the cooling rack along one wall, the burn-test bench beyond it and the packing counter at the sash window, with the deckchair lock-up at the end of the terrace and the five-storey hotel directly opposite.
venues.activity: Everyone is dipping tapers: lifting a frame of wicks off the rail, lowering it into a vat for a slow count, raising it and standing it on the cooling rack, then taking it round again — one thin layer at a time, over and over.

venues.pun_explanation: A taper is a thin candle and a taper is the one instruction this chapter exists to give, and they are the same word, so a working candle shop puts the treatment rule on the fascia in the shop's own honest trade English. The device pays out because everything a taper does physically is what a dose schedule does: the burn-test bench carries a graded run of candles stepping down in height across the board, which is a written withdrawal schedule rendered as an object; and the one at the end that was snapped off and blown out instead of snuffed has flared, scorched the bench and put the fire bucket into the picture — an abrupt stop that turned dangerous, which is precisely why the chapter says withdrawal from this class can kill and alcohol-type withdrawal from any other cannot be assumed milder. The shop rules board carries the never-blow-one-out rule as posted regulation, which is the deontic half of the chapter. Cross-tolerance is a native fact of the trade rather than a metaphor: the same frames of wicks go into any vat on the bench, paraffin, stearin or beeswax, and the spirit bottle kept under the bench for thinning is the fourth thing that fits. venues.place: A high-street pawnbroker's on a Friday afternoon: a long counter with a brass grille, the redemption window at one end, a wall of racked guitars, watches and labelled unredeemed lots behind it, bicycles hung from the ceiling, and the shop door standing open onto the street with the amusement arcade opposite.
venues.activity: Everyone is pawning or redeeming something over the counter: unwrapping a watch out of a tea towel, watching it weighed and put under the loupe, taking a numbered ticket and counting the notes, or handing a ticket back through the grille and waiting while the lot is fetched.

venues.pun_explanation: Both words on the fascia are ordinary pawnbroking and both are the chapter. Chase is a plain surname and chasing losses is the criterion that defines the disorder; a pledge is the object left over the counter and the pledge is what is taken at the Thursday meeting; and a pledge office is genuine trade English for the shop, so nothing on the sign is a joke a real high street would not carry. The venue was chosen over the obvious one because the casino is a fixed course-wide symbol and must stand inside the chapter's world, not replace it — so the world is the shop on the other side of the road, and the traffic between the two is the whole mechanism. Chasing is not asserted, it is drawn: the same watch redeemed and re-pawned, three stubs deep on the same spike, the customer going back out of the door and across. Tolerance is the escalating size of what comes in. The wedding ring in the tray is the relationship criterion and the parent at the counter paying off someone else's ticket is the bailout criterion, both of them literal depiction with no invented glyph. A pawnshop is also the only ordinary venue that keeps an explicit written list of what it will and will not take, which is where the DSM's decision lives: the dice are on the accepted list, and the games console sits in the locked cabinet with a not-yet label on it, because internet gaming is filed for further study rather than admitted. Treatment fits the same furniture — the small ad card in the window for the Thursday back-room meeting, the ledger where what was actually got back is written next to what was paid, and the bolt on the door. The stock inventory is enormous and every item on the shelf is a life someone has already handed over, which is a free fact-slot per object.

venues.place: A municipal model-yacht pond in a park on a Sunday morning: a paved perimeter walk right round the water, a small brick club hut with a glazed noticeboard beside its door, boat trestles set out along the path at wide intervals, and a low concrete island with a single tree standing in the middle of the pond.
venues.activity: Everyone is sailing a model yacht: standing at their own spot on the perimeter walk with a transmitter, trimming a sail, walking a few paces along the coping to follow the boat, lifting it out at the wall to shift the rig, and setting it back on the water.
venues.anchor_structure: The pond's long concrete rim and perimeter walk — the coping, the boat trestles ranged along it and the low island wall beyond — running from the bottom-left corner of the frame to the top right, splitting the scene into the club hut, the near walk, the open water with its island, and the far bank.
venues.pun_explanation: The pond's geometry is the disorder. Twenty people stand round one sheet of water doing exactly the same thing at exactly the same time, each rooted to his own arc of the coping, none of them closer than four paces to the next, and not one boat ever comes alongside another — present, parallel, permanently out of contact, and nobody in the frame is troubled by it. That is the distinction the chapter turns on, and the venue draws it rather than asserting it: the man on the far bank holding a boat he will not put on the water, watching a hut door he will not walk through, is Avoidant and he is plainly suffering; the men on the wall would not notice if the hut were open or shut, and that is Schizoid. The class name on the board does the retrieval work — Solo is a real single-handed class, so the fascia says solitary activities in the sport's own vocabulary without printing a diagnosis. The rest of the criteria are stock: one flask and one cup, a courting couple passing behind the trestles entirely unregistered, nobody smiling at a win, a member who reacts neither to the trophy shelf nor to the protest flag raised against him, and a flat face at a transmitter. The autism differential gets its own figure without a second venue — the member sailing the identical circuit over and over with his tools laid out in a rigid row is restricted and repetitive, which the others are not. Treatment is the coach who stands a deliberate two paces back and passes a spanner across without small talk. And the pond has, as an ordinary municipal feature, a small island with one tree on it, which is where the chapter's fixed glyph stands without being imported.

The criteria that are hardest to draw are the ones the shop supplies best: a donated television, plugged in to prove it works, with its presenter apparently talking straight at the one customer who has stopped dead in front of it, is an idea of reference by literal depiction; the foxed mirror and the crackling transistor are unusual perceptual experiences that anyone can verify are simply a bad mirror and a bad radio, which is the point of the differential — nothing here is actually psychotic, everything works once you wind it. venues.pun_explanation: EXTRA DURABLE is what every luggage shop has had painted across its window since luggage was invented, and it says EXTRADURAL without a clinical word on the glass — dura is a hard-wearing-covering word first and an anatomical one second, which is why the covering was named after it. A hard case is a rigid opaque shell whose contents shift and cannot be seen, so a knock on one corner opening the shell at the corner diagonally opposite is the counter's most ordinary complaint and the mechanism is printed on the sign as the shop's two most ordinary words. The lining is the load-bearing detail and it is real construction: a lining is stitched down along the seams, so anything collecting between shell and lining swells into a tight lens that stops dead at the stitch lines, while anything getting in under the loose lining spreads on round the corner as a long thin crescent and crosses every seam — two shapes, both drawn on the shop's own goods, neither of them a diagram. The case that was checked, passed and set on the shelf an hour ago and has quietly split its seam since is the interval that costs people their lives; the two chrome studs beside the handle with one pushed proud and stuck is the pupil; and the dark stain creeping under the lining behind the top handle is the bruise that appears round the back. venues.activity: Everyone is fitting a timber — taking a plank out of the steam box, bending it round the frames, cramping it home, and leaving it clamped to cool.
venues.anchor_structure: The hull up on the slipway in her cradle, propped along both sides by a row of timber shores, running from the lower-left corner of the yard up to the shed doors at the upper right.
venues.pun_explanation: Pawsey is a real surname over a real family yard and it says palsy; the initial in front of it is the one every such board carries, and the two together read without a clinical word being painted anywhere. The trade was chosen because its central operation is this chapter's whole management in one piece of everyday work: a plank is heated until it yields, bent round the frames, cramped home and left clamped until it cools, and it holds that shape for the life of the boat — while the one unclamped too early springs straight back. Stretching, serial casting and bracing are one job here and nobody calls them anything. The chapter's hardest point is the yard's own standing fact, said in the yard's own words: the line was laid off wrong on the loft floor once, before a single timber was cut, and every frame taken from it carries it; the fault happened at the start, it is finished, it never gets worse — and yet every season the hull is asked to carry more, so the same old set costs more and more shores go on. The five ways a hull is carried through the winter here are the mobility grades as ordinary yard practice, and they describe support and not worth: afloat on her own, afloat with a fender, held on a trot line, up in a cradle, up in a full frame of shores, with the yard board saying which hull is in which because it decides who lifts what tomorrow. Three planks at the bench are the three pictures side by side and they are timber, not people — one so stiff it will not take the bend and has snapped, one so soft it takes any shape and holds none, one that came out of the box with a wave in it and will not lie true. The shores are counted rather than lettered: two under one side, four under a whole hull, one corner packed up on wedges. The halyard of signal flags with its code card is a boat saying exactly what it needs across water it cannot shout over; the generator that trips so the lights go for ten seconds and come back is the yard's own interruption; and the damp streak chalked round in the planking either side of the keelson is what the yard finds in every hull that went in the water before her time.

venues.anchor_structure: The cutaway demonstration roof on its stand in the middle of the yard, its slope and its cut-open courses of tile, batten, felt and deck running from the lower left of the frame to the upper right.
venues.pun_explanation: Tear-a-ply is exactly how this audience says therapy, and both halves are genuine trade words — a tear-off is what you do to the old covering before you can lay anything new, and a ply is one layer of felt in a built-up roof. The merchant earns a survey chapter because six competing schools need six signage slots and a sample bay is a free one: each bay is a whole system for solving the same problem a different way, with its own name board and its own guarantee card, and the years printed on those cards carry the evidence base with nothing invented. The cutaway roof in the middle of the yard is the depth model as an object — visible covering, batten, felt, deck, and the rafters nobody ever sees — and the trade's own rule, that you strip back until you reach sound deck before you decide anything, is the one thing every school in the chapter agrees on. The surveyor holding a moisture meter flat against an unopened panel to read what is going on underneath is mentalization drawn without a word. The oldest bay carries a founder's portrait and a dated plate over a thick multi-ply build-up; the slimmer bay beside it is built off the same deck, which is the family quarrel of the whole chapter, and a sample card at the counter says only that a covering is good enough for the job.

venues.place: A concrete block works and its little testing house on a weekday morning: the mixer and block machine at one end, a long run of curing racks loaded with grey blocks, and a glazed testing room where samples go into the press one at a time.
venues.activity: Everyone is testing the day's batch — carrying a sample block from the racks to the press, winding the load on, and writing the reading on the card.
venues.anchor_structure: The run of curing racks stacked with blocks and the output conveyor feeding it, stepping away from the lower-left corner up to the upper right of the yard, with the compression press standing at its near end.
venues.pun_explanation: C, B and T head the three words of an utterly ordinary trade name — a works that makes cement blocks and tests them — and the three letters are picked out on the fascia the way the corpus picks out expreSS tRIps. The works was chosen because its trade is the method: nobody here argues about whether a block is strong, they put it in the press and wind the load on until it tells them, which is collaborative empiricism and the behavioural experiment in one machine, and the banner over the press says exactly that in the works' own words. A block is only as good as what is under it, so the demonstration slab's foundation course laid to a string line carries core beliefs under automatic thoughts, and the mix docket says what actually went in. The reject pallet holds a dozen blocks each deformed in one named way — one bowed, one twisted, one split clean in two, one short-measured — which is the distortion list as a contrast set rather than a list of words. Three mould boxes stamped in order sit on the bench and are the model everybody teaches first. The press dial is scaled nought to a hundred and is a carrier whose real job is bearing that scale; the loading rig that adds one step weight at a time up a numbered rack is graded exposure with nothing invented; and the half-blocks in the take-one-home bin by the gate are the homework.

venues.place: A demolition site on a terraced street at mid-morning: the block behind already down to clean rubble, the original front wall still standing and held upright by a steel frame of raking shores, a long-reach machine picking at the back, hoses damping the dust down.
venues.activity: Everyone is working the takedown — wetting down, picking the structure apart in the posted order, and sorting what comes off into the right skip.
venues.anchor_structure: The steel frame of raking shores propping the retained front wall, its diagonal legs running from the lower-left pavement up to the head of the wall at the upper right.
venues.pun_explanation: D, B and T head the three words of an ordinary contractor's board, and this contractor's job is the dialectic itself made out of steel. Facade retention is routine, licensed, unremarkable temporary works: the front wall is kept exactly as it is, propped and unchanged, while everything behind it is taken down and rebuilt. It is the only mundane thing that holds acceptance and change true at the same time, and it is what the B on the fascia stands on. The site is not chosen for destruction and nothing here is dramatic — it is a calm, wetted-down, heavily documented morning, and the mnemonic is the propped wall, not the rubble. The rest is the site's own paperwork: the posted sequence of works, numbered and worked strictly top down, is the target hierarchy; the orange tag wired to each prop saying it is temporary and must not be removed is tolerating a load you cannot yet fix; the bowser damping down so nothing flares is regulation; the banksman and the machine driver working one agreed set of hand signals is asking for what you need in a code both sides already have; the four in hi-vis standing round a drawing on a tailgate before anyone touches anything is the consultation meeting; the twenty-four-hour number on the hoarding is the between-session call; the permit board with its slots and its pen on a string is the diary card; and the rigger walking a lifting chain link by link with a paint stick, marking the one link that let go, is a chain analysis drawn exactly.

venues.place: A river rowing club on an ordinary Saturday outing: the boathouse doors folded back on tiered racks of hulls, a timber landing raft running out from the doors into the stream, a worn concrete slipway beside it, a rack of blades stood on their handles against the wall, and a run of numbered landing stages spaced along the bank upstream.
venues.activity: Everyone is getting a boat onto the water and pulling away from the raft — carrying a hull down on shoulders, setting the blades into the gates, holding a boat steady while a crew steps in, pushing off, sitting to the oars and pulling.
venues.anchor_structure: The timber landing raft and its ramp — a long staging running out from the boathouse doors across the shallows into the stream — cutting the frame from the lower left to the upper right and dividing it into the boathouse, the hard, the raft and the open water.
venues.pun_explanation: O-A-R-S stand in order as the word-initials of a completely genuine river-club name — the expreSS tRIps device — and OARS is the method's own four-skill acronym, so the fascia is the club and the syllabus at once. The trade then hands over the model without a single invented image. The cox is the whole spirit of the method made ordinary: he sits facing the crew, holds no oar, cannot move a heavy hull an inch himself, and gets it off the raft entirely by asking and calling — partnership rather than expertise, and the client does every stroke of the pulling. A double scull, two people pulling one boat and neither able to move it alone, is that partnership again. The stages of change are the numbered landing stages along the bank: they are come up in order, a boat may lie at one for as long as it likes, and a boat that stops pulling drifts back down past the stages it has already passed, which is relapse drawn as ordinary river behaviour instead of as a wheel diagram. Rolling with resistance is the club's first coaching point, painted on the river-rules board: you do not fight the stream, you lean the boat and let the water carry it round, and the crew shoving against the current sits still in the middle of the frame going nowhere. Four blades to a bay in the rack outside the door are the four skills; four boats going out in order behind the launch are the four processes.

venues.place: A canal lock staircase on a busy summer morning: five stone chambers stepping up the hillside one straight into the next, black-and-white balance beams swung out over the towpath, a lock-keeper's hut with a toll window beside the bottom gate, a line of boats waiting their turn along the bank below, and side ponds and an overflow weir running down beside the flight.
venues.activity: Everyone is working a boat up through the locks — winding a paddle up on a windlass, walking a balance beam open with their back against it, holding a rope round a bollard while the chamber fills, walking the boat forward into the next chamber.
venues.anchor_structure: The flight of five chambers with its balance beams — a stepped run of stone walls and timber gates climbing the hillside — cutting the frame from the lower left to the upper right and dividing it into the waiting line below, the chambers themselves, the towpath and the keeper's hut.
venues.pun_explanation: A staircase lock is the continuum of care built in stone. A boat is lifted one level at a time, no level can be skipped, it can only be taken up when the level above is ready to receive it, and it comes back down the same way it went up — which is the step-up and step-down criteria drawn as ordinary canal work rather than as a ladder diagram. Five chambers give the five settings in order from the open pound at the bottom, through the two shallow middle chambers, to the top chamber with the deepest walls and the gates shut behind it. The keeper is the case manager: he owns no boat, and decides only who enters, in what order, and how long each lies in the pound. Every remaining item is a real fitting on a real flight. Milieu is the posted routine on the hut wall — operating hours, the order of working, the rule that no boat enters alone. The token economy is literally a token economy, because tolls on the cut were paid in numbered brass checks and the keeper's board is hung with them. Restraint is the moment this chapter is careful about, and the flight makes it ordinary, brief and bounded: while the chamber is filling and the water is at its most turbulent the boat is held short on two ropes round the bollards, by two people, for exactly as long as the level is unsettled, and let go the moment it settles. Stop planks stacked against the wall are crisis containment; the bypass channel and the weir carry all the water that never needs a chamber at all, which is the least restrictive route; the side ponds hold what the flight cannot; and a boat coming back down past the waiting line is readmission.

venues.place: A municipal playing field on a Sunday-morning youth training session: two pitches marked out on one field, portable goals, a rail and hoarding line along the touchline with parents behind it, and a low brick changing block with its street number by the door.
venues.activity: Everyone is running the same warm-up drill — the whole squad working through the coach's grid of cones in turn.
venues.anchor_structure: The touchline rail with its run of sponsor hoardings, carrying from the lower-left corner of the field up to the changing block at the upper right, a portable goal standing at its far end.
venues.pun_explanation: I, E and P head the three words of a completely ordinary municipal ground name — grounds really are named for the corner of the parish they sit in — so the education plan every child psychiatrist is examined on becomes the largest lettering in the frame with no medical word on it, and the changing block's own street number carries the other plan without inventing a prop. The ground was chosen because tiered prevention is what youth coaching already does and can be seen doing: the whole squad in one colour of bib working the same grid, a small group pulled aside to a second grid in a second colour, one child working one-to-one with a coach at the far goal in a third — all three tiers visible at once, in one frame, at the same session. Accommodation is this trade's own habit too: a smaller ball, a lower goal and a longer run at it for the child who needs one, with the adaptation card pinned to the kit bag. The registration table under the awning issuing a pass that lets a child play out of his age band is the eligibility and placement committee; the welfare officer's sealed envelope of forms, opened to the coach only as far as it says what he must actually do, is confidentiality against need-to-know; the conduct board on the rail and the line the parents must stand behind are the behaviour code; the visiting coach signing the clipboard at the gate is the consultant arriving from outside the system; and the scout at the rail writing one name down is early identification and referral.

venues.title_en: Psychodynamic: Anna Freud, Klein, Kohut, Mentalization
venues.place: A puppet-maker's workshop on the evening shift: a long carving bench of vices and glue pots down the middle, an overhead stringing rail above it hung with marionettes on control bars, a wall of shallow parts trays to the ceiling, a full-length rehearsal mirror at the far end and wood shavings underfoot.
venues.activity: Everyone is making a puppet — carving and gluing at the bench, painting faces at the paint end, knotting strings up to the rail, and working a finished one by hand in front of the mirror.
venues.anchor_structure: The long carving bench with the overhead stringing rail running above it, corner to corner from lower-left to upper-right down the whole depth of the room, splitting the frame into parts-tray wall / bench / stringing rail / mirror end.
venues.pun_explanation: KLEIN is the theorist's surname used exactly as a maker's trade name is used, and for this audience it is also simply the word small — a workshop that makes small people. The workshop then pays the rest of the chapter out of its own furniture without inventing anything. Klein's part-objects are the shallow trays sorted by part: a tray of heads, a tray of hands, a tray of glass eyes, the object existing only in pieces; the depressive position is the mending bench where a snapped puppet is clamped and glued back into one whole thing, which is Klein's own word, reparation. Anna Freud's hierarchy of defences is the three-step drying rack, rough blanks at the bottom, varnished faces on top. Kohut's three selfobject needs are three ordinary workshop pairings: a maker holding a puppet up to the mirror, an apprentice under the tall maestro marionette hung highest on the rail, and two identical twins sharing one control bar. And mentalization is the trade itself — a hand up inside a hollow head, a fixed wooden face that has no mind of its own, and a second person who must read one into it and answer it.

venues.place: A municipal public lending library on a wet afternoon: a long issue desk with a date-stamp block, a returns chute and its trolley, tall shelving bays running back into the room, a card-catalogue cabinet on the end wall and a low children's corner behind a half-gate.
venues.activity: Everyone is borrowing and returning books — browsing the bays, carrying an armful to the desk to be date-stamped, emptying the returns trolley and shelving what came back.
venues.anchor_structure: The long issue desk with the returns trolley run beside it and the tall shelving bays behind, running lower-left to upper-right across the room and splitting the frame into returns chute and entrance / issue desk / open bays / children's corner and closed stacks.
venues.pun_explanation: A lending library is the only ordinary building whose entire trade is objects leaving their owner and coming back, which is what the chapter is about, and the sign carries the theorist's name the way every municipal library carries its donor's. The mapping is exact and free: object constancy is the card-catalogue drawer, where a card stands for a book that is not on the shelf and is not lost — the internal representation of an absent object, filed in alphabetical order. Mahler's whole sequence is the loan cycle: the toddler in the children's corner who carries one picture book out to a parent at the desk and straight back to the low shelf is practicing and refuelling; the RESERVED shelf behind the desk holds a named item until its owner comes, which is Winnicott's holding, and the taped, mended, much-borrowed picture book still in circulation is good-enough. The transitional object is that same book, refused at the desk by the child who brought it in. True and false self is the bright dust jacket over the drab cloth board underneath. Kernberg gets the returns desk: two triage trays, one to re-shelve and one to withdraw, with nothing allowed in between, and a trolley of spine-labelless books that belong to no section at all.

venues.title_en: Later theorists: Erikson, Bion, Ogden, Lacan, Spitz, Stern, relational
venues.place: A bellhanging works on a fitting-out day: the trial frame standing down the middle of the shed with a graded ring of eight bells bolted into it, wheels and headstocks laid out on the boards beneath, a vertical tuning lathe at one end with a bell mouth-up under the cutter, an inspection and lettering bench along the window wall, and the ropes dropping through the floor holes into the pit below.
venues.activity: Everyone is fitting out and sounding bells — bolting a bell onto its headstock, hanging its wheel and rope, cutting metal off one on the tuning lathe, and striking each bell with a hand hammer to hear it.
venues.anchor_structure: The timber-and-steel trial frame carrying the ring of eight bells, running from the lathe end at lower left up to the yard doors at upper right, the largest thing in the shed, splitting the frame into the tuning lathe and its swarf / the eight bells in the frame / the lettering and inspection bench along the windows / the rope pit and the open yard doors.
venues.pun_explanation: A bell is a hollow container whose entire job is to take a raw meaningless blow from a clapper held inside it and hand it back as a note — Bion's container-contained and alpha-function are the physical operation of the trade, so the works carries his name on its board the way the corpus lets a barbershop carry barbiturates. Everything else the chapter tests is then ordinary bellhanging stock. A ring is eight bells graded by size, numbered on their headstocks and rung strictly from treble to tenor with no bell skipped, which is Erikson's fixed epigenetic sequence; the one bell whose inscription band is still blank, with its loose letters spilled across the bench, is identity versus role confusion. A bell sounds five partials at once and none of them replaces the one below it — Stern's layered senses of self — and the tuner brings them in by striking a fork, laying his palm flat on the metal and cutting until fork and bell agree, which is affect attunement working across two senses at once; the instant two bells strike dead together is the moment of meeting, and the beat tone two mistuned bells make, belonging to neither of them, is Ogden's analytic third, while the hand run slowly over the polished soundbow feeling for a flaw is the autistic-contiguous surface. The bright band on that soundbow gives a whole curved figure back to whoever leans over it, which is Lacan's mirror stage, and one bell carries his three orders as three bands: the reflecting one, the cast inscription of raised letters, and the rough unmachined crown nobody finishes. The dull green bell standing unhung in the corner with its clapper hanging on a nail is Spitz's hospitalism; a bell puts its whole weight on the headstock it leans on, so the one lying on its side with the headstock off is the anaclitic case; and the muffle box gives protest, despair and detachment as one bell open, one half-muffled and one with its clapper tied. Every rope drops through the same floor holes into one pit, so two crossed ropes pulling two men off balance, neither of them having meant it, is the two-person field and the enactment.

venues.place: A model flying club's field on a bright Sunday morning: a mown grass strip with a white-painted flight line along it, marked pilot boxes on the grass, a row of pits bays behind with models on trestles, a timber clubhouse with a peg board by its door, and a boundary hedge with the far side of the valley beyond it.
venues.activity: Everyone is flying a radio-controlled model — standing in a marked box on the line with a transmitter held at the waist, thumbs on the sticks, eyes up on their own model out over the field.
venues.anchor_structure: The mown grass strip with its white-painted flight line and the low crowd barrier running beside it, cutting from the pits at lower left to the boundary hedge at upper right, the largest thing in the frame, splitting it into clubhouse and peg board / pits bays and charging bench / pilot boxes on the line / the strip and the ground beyond the boundary.
venues.pun_explanation: Tele- is the chapter's own first morpheme and it means at a distance, so a club whose field is called Telescope Hill reads as a genuine club name, keeps the morpheme, and says far-seeing without printing the topic. The whole hobby is the chapter's literal picture: the pilot never touches the thing he is responsible for, works entirely by watching a small figure play at a distance, and everything can go wrong at the far end of a link. Every fact then hangs on ordinary field furniture. The peg board by the hut door, where you must take your channel's peg before switching on or two sets clash and both models come down, is the shared insecure channel, and the bind plug taped inside one transmitter is the paired encrypted link. The buddy-box lead joining an instructor's set to a beginner's, so the adult can take control on the instant, is the parent in the room and the supervising clinician on the line at once. The canvas windbreak screening one pits bay is the private space the child is entitled to, and the spotter standing at a pilot's shoulder is the second pair of eyes the remote observer does not have. The laminated card wired to the gate giving the field's exact location, beside the pinned emergency plan and the first-aid box, is the rule that you establish where the patient physically is before the session starts; the owner's name-and-address label in an open fuselage hatch, the failsafe setting and the lost-model alarm beeping out in the long grass beyond the hedge are what you do once the link is already gone, and the retrieval barrow is the fetch. The thirty-pace range-check stake is the technology check before you begin. The boundary hedge and its line of posts, which no model may be flown across, is licensure and jurisdiction, and the affiliation certificate screwed up in the hut is the licence itself. The proficiency-certificate board with names and dates on it is the evidence base, the signing-in book and the clipboard of forms are consent, and the laptop running a simulator on the trestle table inside the hut is the app used between sessions and never instead of them.

venues.place: An assay office on a busy trade morning: a long testing bench down the middle with a rack of acid bottles and a row of beam balances, a black touchstone slab at the near end, a hallmark punch press at the far end, and a brass-grilled trade counter where jewellers hand in numbered trays.
venues.activity: Everyone is testing metal — scraping a sample off an item, drawing the streak across the touchstone, dropping acid on it, weighing it on the balance and punching the mark.
venues.anchor_structure: The long testing bench with its rack of acid bottles and its row of beam balances, running lower-left to upper-right the length of the room and splitting the frame into trade counter / testing bench / punch press / reject drawers and street window.
venues.pun_explanation: Every idiom this chapter speaks in is already an assay-office noun, so the venue is the plain-English picture of the field's own vocabulary: the gold standard, the weight of evidence, levels and grades, the acid test, and appraisal, which is what an assayer literally does — an assay is a trial in the oldest sense of the word. The office then hands over its stock as free fact slots. The fineness chart on the wall is a ladder of grades from coarsest to purest, which is the hierarchy of evidence with the top grade at the top. The acid bottles are the test that either holds or does not. The loupe is critical appraisal, the beam balance with its fitted case of certified weights is weight of evidence, and the sealed sample envelopes with the owner's name folded out of sight are blinding. The crucible where scrapings from many separate trays are combined into one reading is pooling. The chalk tally counts items tested against items passed. The half-open reject drawer under the bench, full of unstamped pieces that never reach the window display, is publication bias, and the hallmark punch itself is the approval stamp, so an unstamped piece still being sold at the counter is off-label. The one joke the venue tells for free is the ring mandrel, where an adult ring is being cut down to fit a child's finger and re-tested.
